questions.question: A team classifies its fraud-detection system as "high-risk" under the EU AI Act. Which consequence follows most directly?

options.A: The system is prohibited from being placed on the market
options.B: The system must meet obligations such as risk management, data governance, logging, human oversight, and conformity assessment
options.C: The system is exempt from all documentation requirements
options.D: Only the training data needs to be encrypted

questions.explanation: High-risk AI systems are permitted but carry heavy obligations: risk management processes, data governance, technical documentation, record-keeping, transparency, human oversight, and conformity assessment before deployment.

questions.question: Which situation best illustrates why an AI-based system may need re-testing even though its code has not changed?

options.A: The CI pipeline was upgraded
options.B: The model was retrained on newer data, changing its predictions
options.C: A new tester joined the team

questions.explanation: In ML systems the model, not just the code, determines behaviour. Retraining produces a new model that must be re-verified regardless of code changes.

questions.question: A product owner says "our chatbot is AI, so it cannot have bugs, only training issues." What is the best tester response?

options.A: Agree; AI systems have no defects
options.B: Explain that AI-based systems have both conventional defects (in surrounding code, integration, data pipelines) and model-related problems, and both need testing

questions.explanation: An AI-based system is mostly conventional software around a model. Defects can occur in APIs, pre/post-processing, prompts, and data flow, in addition to model-quality issues.

questions.question: Which characteristic most distinguishes a machine-learning approach from a rule-based (expert-system) approach to the same classification task?

options.A: ML derives its decision logic from data rather than from explicitly coded rules
options.B: ML cannot be wrong

questions.explanation: A rule-based system encodes human-authored rules; an ML system infers a model from examples. This shifts the testing focus toward data quality and statistical behaviour.

questions.question: A safety-critical AI feature must allow an operator to disable it instantly. Which AI quality characteristic does this requirement primarily address, and which stakeholder concern does it serve?

options.A: Portability; serving deployment teams
options.B: Intervenability (user controllability); serving safety and accountability

questions.explanation: The ability for a human to intervene or stop the system is intervenability/user controllability, and it directly supports safety and legal accountability.

questions.question: Why does non-determinism complicate defect reproduction for a generative AI system, and what is a practical mitigation during testing?

options.A: It does not; just rerun the test
options.B: Identical prompts may not reproduce the failure; fixing the random seed and decoding parameters (for example temperature 0) improves reproducibility
options.C: Non-determinism only affects performance, not results; no mitigation is needed
options.D: The only fix is to retrain the model

questions.explanation: Sampling makes outputs vary. Pinning the seed and using greedy or low-temperature decoding makes runs repeatable enough to investigate and regression-test a defect.

questions.question: A recruitment model shows 92% accuracy overall but selects far fewer qualified female candidates than male ones. Which quality characteristic is most clearly violated?

options.A: Efficiency
options.B: Fairness / freedom from unwanted bias

questions.explanation: High aggregate accuracy can mask group-level unfairness. The disparity in favourable outcomes across gender indicates a bias/fairness problem.

questions.question: Which test would most directly assess the robustness of an image classifier?

options.A: Measuring inference latency at peak load
options.B: Adding small perturbations, blur, brightness shifts, and adversarial noise to inputs and checking that predictions remain stable and correct
options.C: Counting the number of model parameters
options.D: Checking that the API returns HTTP 200

questions.explanation: Robustness testing perturbs inputs within realistic and adversarial bounds and verifies that outputs do not degrade unacceptably.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks for "explainability" of a credit-scoring model. Which deliverable best satisfies a local explanation requirement?

options.A: Overall model accuracy on the test set
options.B: For each individual decision, the main input features that drove that specific outcome (for example via SHAP values)
options.D: The cloud region where the model runs

questions.explanation: A local explanation attributes a single prediction to its most influential features. Global metrics like accuracy do not explain individual decisions.

questions.question: Which pair of AI quality characteristics can be in tension, requiring a documented trade-off decision?

options.A: Explainability and predictive performance (a simpler, more explainable model may be less accurate)
options.B: Installability and portability

questions.explanation: Highly accurate models (deep networks, large ensembles) are often opaque, while inherently interpretable models may sacrifice accuracy. The chosen balance should be justified against the use context.

questions.question: How should acceptance criteria for an ML classifier's functional performance normally be expressed?

options.A: As a single pass/fail on one hand-picked example
options.B: As target values for chosen metrics (for example recall >= 0.95, precision >= 0.80) measured on a representative, held-out dataset
options.C: As the number of lines of training code
options.D: As the number of features used

questions.explanation: Because behaviour is statistical, acceptance criteria set quantitative thresholds on relevant metrics, evaluated on data representative of production.

questions.question: A medical triage model must never miss a critical case, even at the cost of extra false alarms. Which metric target reflects this best?

options.A: Maximise precision, accept low recall
options.B: Maximise recall for the critical class, accept lower precision

questions.explanation: Missing a critical case is a false negative. Prioritising recall for that class reduces false negatives, accepting more false positives (lower precision).

questions.question: Which is the clearest example of testing the "transparency" of an AI-based system?

options.A: Verifying that users are informed they are interacting with an AI and what data it uses
options.B: Measuring the model's F1-score

questions.explanation: Transparency includes disclosure: users should know they are dealing with AI, and how their data and the outputs are used.

questions.question: During robustness testing, a self-driving perception model misclassifies stop signs when small stickers are added. This is best categorised as a failure of:

options.A: Functional correctness only
options.B: Robustness against adversarial / real-world perturbations, with a safety impact

questions.explanation: Sensitivity to physically realisable perturbations is a robustness weakness, and in this context it directly threatens safety.

questions.question: Which statement about testing "functional adaptability" of an adaptive AI system is correct?

options.A: It can be tested once before release and never again
options.B: It requires ongoing evaluation because the system changes behaviour in response to new data or environments
options.D: It is identical to load testing

questions.explanation: Functional adaptability means behaviour changes with context, so verification must continue in operation, not stop at release.

questions.question: A model scores 0.99 accuracy on training data and 0.71 on the validation set. What is the most likely diagnosis and a reasonable first action?

options.A: Underfitting; add more model capacity
options.B: Overfitting; apply regularisation, more/augmented data, or reduce model complexity
options.C: Data leakage into training; no action needed
options.D: The metric is wrong; ignore it

questions.explanation: A large train-validation gap signals overfitting. Regularisation, early stopping, more data, or a simpler model typically reduce the gap.

questions.question: A tester notices that a feature "account_id" strongly predicts churn in the training data. Why is this a concern?

options.A: It is not a concern; high predictive power is always good
options.B: It is likely target leakage or an identifier that will not generalise, giving over-optimistic results
options.C: Account IDs must always be one-hot encoded
options.D: It means the model is too simple

questions.explanation: An identifier that correlates with the label usually indicates leakage or memorisation. It inflates offline metrics but fails on new accounts.

questions.question: For a spam filter with 5% spam prevalence, the model achieves precision 0.60 and recall 0.90 on the spam class. What does this mean operationally?

options.A: 90% of predicted-spam messages are actually spam
options.B: The filter catches 90% of real spam, but 40% of messages it flags as spam are actually legitimate
options.C: The filter is 95% accurate on all messages, so it is fine
options.D: Precision and recall cannot both be reported

questions.explanation: Recall 0.90 = catches 90% of real spam. Precision 0.60 = 60% of flagged items are truly spam, so 40% are false positives, a real usability risk.

questions.question: Which use of a ROC curve and its AUC is appropriate?

options.A: Comparing classifiers' ability to separate classes across all decision thresholds
options.B: Measuring training time

questions.explanation: ROC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate over thresholds; AUC summarises threshold-independent separability, useful for comparing models.

questions.question: A team uses k-fold cross-validation. What is its main benefit over a single train/validation split?

options.A: It removes the need for a test set
options.B: It gives a more stable performance estimate by averaging over multiple folds, reducing dependence on one particular split

questions.explanation: Cross-validation reduces variance in the performance estimate by rotating which data is held out, though a separate final test set is still advisable.

questions.question: When is fine-tuning a pretrained model preferable to using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?

options.A: When the knowledge changes daily and must always be current
options.B: When you need the model to adopt a consistent style, format, or task behaviour that is hard to specify in a prompt
options.C: When you cannot afford any training compute
options.D: When you want to avoid changing model weights

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning bakes in behaviour/style/format. RAG is better for frequently changing factual knowledge because documents can be updated without retraining.

questions.question: A classifier's default threshold is 0.5. Business wants fewer false negatives. Which threshold change and side effect is correct?

options.A: Raise the threshold; recall increases, precision decreases
options.B: Lower the threshold; recall increases, precision typically decreases
options.C: Lower the threshold; both precision and recall increase
options.D: Threshold has no effect on precision or recall

questions.explanation: Lowering the positive-class threshold labels more items positive, catching more true positives (higher recall) but also more false positives (lower precision).

questions.question: Which is a correct description of "hyperparameter tuning" and where its results should be measured?

options.A: Adjusting learned weights, measured on the training set
options.B: Searching configuration values such as depth or learning rate, with candidates compared on the validation set (not the test set)
options.C: Changing the loss function at inference time

questions.explanation: Hyperparameters are set outside training. Comparing configurations on the validation set avoids contaminating the final, held-out test set.

questions.question: In an LLM, raising the "temperature" parameter tends to:

options.A: Make outputs more deterministic and repetitive
options.B: Increase randomness and diversity of the generated text

questions.explanation: Temperature scales the probability distribution before sampling. Higher values flatten it, producing more varied (and less predictable) outputs.

questions.question: A tester must evaluate an embedding-based semantic search feature. Which check is most relevant?

options.A: That the SQL schema is normalised
options.B: That semantically similar queries and documents have high vector similarity and are ranked near the top (for example measured with recall@k)
options.C: That the model file is under 1 GB
options.D: That the UI uses the brand colours

questions.explanation: Semantic search quality is judged by whether relevant items are retrieved for a query, using ranking metrics like recall@k, precision@k, or MRR.

questions.question: Why might a team choose a simpler logistic-regression model over a gradient-boosted ensemble even if the ensemble is 2% more accurate?

options.A: Simpler models cannot overfit
options.B: Interpretability, easier monitoring, lower latency, and regulatory explainability requirements may outweigh a small accuracy gain

questions.explanation: Model selection weighs accuracy against explainability, latency, maintainability, and compliance. A modest accuracy loss can be an acceptable trade for transparency.

questions.question: A model is trained with class weights because 1 in 200 transactions is fraudulent. What problem is this addressing?

options.A: Data drift
options.B: Class imbalance, so the minority (fraud) class is not ignored by the learner

questions.explanation: Class weighting (or resampling) counteracts imbalance so the model is penalised more for missing rare positives.

questions.question: Which statement about the training, validation, and test datasets is correct?

options.A: The test set may be used repeatedly to pick the best model
options.B: The test set should be used only once, at the end, for a final unbiased estimate
options.C: Validation and test sets must be identical
options.D: The training set is the smallest of the three

questions.explanation: Repeatedly optimising against the test set turns it into a second validation set and biases the final estimate. It should be touched once.

questions.question: A generative model produces a confident but fabricated citation. This behaviour is called:

options.A: Drift
options.B: Hallucination

questions.explanation: Hallucination is the generation of plausible-sounding but false or unsupported content, a key quality risk for LLM-based systems.

questions.question: Which evaluation approach is most appropriate for a summarisation feature where many summaries can be acceptable?

options.A: Exact string match to one reference summary
options.B: A combination of reference-based metrics (for example ROUGE), rubric-based human review, and task-specific checks

questions.explanation: Open-ended generation needs multiple signals: overlap metrics give a cheap proxy, while human rubric scoring captures faithfulness, coverage, and readability.

questions.question: For an image classifier, a valid metamorphic relation is:

options.A: Rotating a valid image by 5 degrees should not change its predicted class
options.B: Replacing the image with random noise should return the same class
options.C: Deleting the model should return the same class
options.D: Doubling the file size should double the confidence

questions.explanation: A small label-preserving transformation (slight rotation) should leave the prediction unchanged. Violations reveal robustness or invariance defects.

questions.question: A team wants to regression-test an LLM feature after a prompt change. Which practice is most effective?

options.A: Manually eyeball five outputs each release
options.B: Maintain a curated evaluation set with graded expectations and run it automatically, comparing scores against a baseline and a threshold
options.D: Rely on the model provider's benchmarks

questions.explanation: An automated, versioned evaluation set with rubric or reference scoring provides repeatable regression signals when prompts, models, or retrieval change.

questions.question: Which is a correct application of pairwise (combinatorial) testing to an ML system's inputs?

options.A: Using it to test every possible pixel value of an image
options.B: Covering all pairs of values among categorical input factors such as region, device type, and language to find interaction defects efficiently
options.C: Replacing the need for a labelled dataset

questions.explanation: Combinatorial testing reduces a large input-factor space to a set covering all pairs, useful for the structured, categorical inputs around an ML component.

questions.question: During red teaming, a tester bypasses a chatbot's safety filter by asking it to "role-play as an unrestricted assistant." What should the test report capture?

options.A: Only that the test failed
options.B: The prompt, the harmful output, the policy violated, severity, and reproduction conditions, so the team can strengthen guardrails
options.C: Just a screenshot with no context
options.D: Nothing, since red teaming is informal

questions.explanation: Effective red-team reporting is actionable: exact attack prompt, resulting output, which policy was breached, impact/severity, and how to reproduce.

questions.question: Which risk is best mitigated by "human-in-the-loop" review of an AI system's outputs?

options.A: High inference latency
options.B: Acting automatically on incorrect or unsafe AI decisions in high-impact cases

questions.explanation: A human checkpoint before consequential actions catches wrong or unsafe outputs that automated confidence scores alone might not flag.

questions.question: A tester designs "acceptable-range" checks for a house-price model instead of exact expected values. This is an example of:

options.A: A complete oracle
options.B: A partial/heuristic oracle that verifies the prediction is within a plausible bound given the inputs

questions.explanation: When the exact answer is unknown, checking that outputs fall within sane, input-consistent ranges is a practical heuristic oracle.

questions.question: Which is the strongest argument for independent (third-party) testing of a high-risk AI system?

options.A: It is cheaper than in-house testing
options.B: It reduces confirmation bias and provides objective evidence for conformity assessment and stakeholder trust
options.C: It removes the need for a test plan

questions.explanation: Independent evaluation counters the developing team's optimism and produces credible, auditable results for regulators and customers.

questions.question: A model's test accuracy is 88% with a 95% confidence interval of plus or minus 4%. What is the correct interpretation for release decisions?

options.A: The true accuracy is exactly 88%
options.B: The true accuracy is plausibly between about 84% and 92%; if the acceptance threshold is 90%, the result is not conclusively met
options.D: Accuracy will always be at least 92% in production

questions.explanation: The interval expresses estimation uncertainty from sample size. A point estimate below the threshold with an interval straddling it does not demonstrate the criterion is satisfied.

questions.question: Which activity best fits the ML "input data" test level rather than the "model" test level?

options.A: Measuring the trained model's precision on a hold-out set
options.B: Checking the training dataset for missing values, duplicates, outliers, label errors, and class balance before training
options.C: Running adversarial attacks against the deployed model
options.D: A/B testing two models in production

questions.explanation: Input data testing evaluates the dataset itself. Model testing evaluates the resulting trained model's behaviour.

questions.question: A GenAI feature summarises legal documents. Which test most directly targets "faithfulness" (no unsupported claims)?

options.A: Checking response time under load
options.B: Verifying every statement in the summary is entailed by the source document, flagging any added or contradicted facts
options.C: Counting the tokens in the output
options.D: Checking the output language is English

questions.explanation: Faithfulness/groundedness testing checks that the summary contains only content supported by the source, catching hallucinated or altered facts.

questions.question: Why is coverage of the operational design domain (ODD) important when testing an autonomous system?

options.A: It defines the UI theme
options.B: It bounds the conditions the system is designed to handle, so tests must cover that space and confirm safe behaviour at and beyond its edges
options.C: It sets the training batch size
options.D: It is only relevant to marketing

questions.explanation: The ODD specifies environments and scenarios (weather, road types, speeds). Test design should cover the ODD thoroughly and verify graceful degradation outside it.

questions.question: A tester proposes using the model under test as its own oracle by checking self-consistency across paraphrased prompts. What is the main limitation?

options.A: It cannot be automated
options.B: Consistent answers can still be consistently wrong, so it detects instability but not systematic errors

questions.explanation: Self-consistency checks find variability, but a model that is confidently and uniformly incorrect will pass. It must be combined with reference or human checks.

questions.question: Which is an appropriate exit criterion for testing an ML classifier before release?

options.A: All unit tests for the web framework pass
options.B: Target metrics met on a representative hold-out set, fairness checks within tolerance, robustness tests passed, and known high-severity risks mitigated
options.C: The model file was produced without error

questions.explanation: AI exit criteria combine statistical performance, fairness, robustness, and risk coverage, not just "the build succeeded."

questions.question: A regression suite for an ML system should be re-run primarily when:

options.A: The office network changes
options.B: The model, training data, feature pipeline, prompts, or dependent libraries change
options.C: A new logo is added to the site

questions.explanation: Any change to the elements that determine model behaviour, data, features, model, prompts, or key libraries, warrants regression testing.

questions.question: When testing a recommendation system, which metric best reflects user-facing quality rather than raw model fit?

options.A: Training loss
options.B: Online engagement measures such as click-through or conversion from an A/B test, alongside offline ranking metrics

questions.explanation: Offline ranking metrics are proxies; controlled online experiments measure the actual effect on user behaviour.

questions.question: A tester finds the LLM answers correctly in English but poorly in Spanish. This is best logged as:

options.A: A performance defect
options.B: A functional-performance gap for a specific input segment (language), with data on the affected slice

questions.explanation: Slice-based analysis reveals that aggregate metrics hide poor performance on a subgroup. The defect report should quantify the affected segment.

questions.question: Which is the best reason to include "negative" and "out-of-scope" prompts in an LLM test set?

options.A: To increase the token count
options.B: To verify the system refuses or safely handles requests it should not answer, rather than only testing happy-path questions

questions.explanation: Safety and scope adherence require testing refusals, disclaimers, and safe fallbacks, not just correct answers to in-scope questions.

questions.question: A model card is most useful to a tester because it documents:

options.A: The office seating plan
options.B: Intended use, training data characteristics, evaluation results, known limitations, and ethical considerations

questions.explanation: A model card summarises intended use, data, metrics by subgroup, and limitations, helping testers design relevant tests and spot misuse risks.

questions.question: Which testing approach directly addresses the risk that an LLM leaks sensitive text from its training data or context?

options.A: Latency profiling
options.B: Data-extraction / prompt-leakage testing, using crafted prompts that try to elicit memorised or system-prompt content

questions.explanation: Targeted prompts probe for memorised PII, secrets, or exposure of the hidden system prompt and retrieved context.

questions.question: A tester wants to prioritise test effort on an ML system using risk-based testing. Which factor pair should drive prioritisation?

options.A: Model file size and framework version
options.B: Likelihood of a failure mode and the impact/severity if it occurs (for example a wrong medical dose)
options.C: Number of developers and sprint length

questions.explanation: Risk-based testing focuses on failure modes with the highest combination of probability and consequence.

questions.question: Which statement about test automation for AI-based systems is most accurate?

options.A: Assertions can rarely be exact equality; they often check metrics, ranges, invariants, or metamorphic relations against thresholds
options.B: Automation is impossible because outputs vary
options.C: Only the UI can be automated
options.D: Automated AI tests never need maintenance

questions.explanation: Automated AI checks typically assert on aggregate metrics, acceptable ranges, invariance/metamorphic properties, or comparisons to a baseline, rather than a single expected string.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A dataset for a global product contains 95% English text. What is the most likely test finding and its consequence?

options.A: The data is fine; language does not matter
options.B: Under-representation of other languages, likely causing poor performance for non-English users in production

questions.explanation: A skewed language distribution means the model learns mostly English patterns and will likely underperform on the under-represented segments.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Which is a sound way to test for label correctness at scale?

options.A: Assume all labels are correct if the file opens
options.B: Sample records for expert re-annotation, measure inter-annotator agreement, and use model-disagreement or confident-learning heuristics to surface likely errors
options.C: Delete all records the model gets wrong

questions.explanation: Label quality is assessed by re-labelling samples, measuring agreement (for example Cohen's kappa), and flagging suspicious items via model disagreement.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: "Data leakage" between training and test sets typically shows up as:

options.A: Offline metrics that are excellent but do not hold up in production
options.B: The training job crashing

questions.explanation: Leakage lets the model 'see' test information (for example duplicated rows or a future-derived feature), inflating offline scores that then collapse on genuinely unseen data.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A tester checks that a time-series model's train/test split is chronological rather than random. Why?

options.A: Random splits look nicer
options.B: A random split lets the model train on future data and be tested on past data, leaking information and overstating performance
options.C: Chronological splits are faster to compute

questions.explanation: For temporal data, evaluation must respect time order so the model is only tested on data that comes after what it learned from.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Which is the best example of testing a data pipeline (as opposed to the model)?

options.A: Checking model precision on a hold-out set
options.B: Verifying that feature transformations applied at training time are identical to those applied at inference time (no train/serve skew)
options.D: Comparing two model versions in production

questions.explanation: Train/serve skew, different preprocessing in training versus serving, is a classic pipeline defect that silently degrades production accuracy.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A fairness review must choose a metric. "Equal opportunity" requires that:

options.A: All groups receive the same number of positive predictions
options.B: True-positive rates are equal across groups (equally good at identifying real positives)

questions.explanation: Equal opportunity is parity of true-positive rate between groups. Different fairness definitions (demographic parity, equalised odds) can conflict and must be chosen deliberately.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Removing the protected attribute (for example ethnicity) from the training data:

options.A: Guarantees the model is fair
options.B: Does not guarantee fairness, because other features can act as proxies for the protected attribute

questions.explanation: "Fairness through unawareness" is weak: correlated features (postcode, name, purchase history) can reconstruct the protected attribute, so bias testing is still required.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A tester should treat a sudden change in a categorical feature's value distribution in incoming data as:

options.A: Always harmless
options.B: A potential data-drift signal that warrants investigation and possibly model re-evaluation
options.C: A reason to delete the feature immediately

questions.explanation: Distribution shifts in production inputs can degrade a model trained on the old distribution; monitoring should raise an alert for investigation.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Synthetic data is proposed to fill gaps for a rare failure class. Which risk should the tester highlight?

options.A: Synthetic data cannot be stored
options.B: If the synthetic data does not match real-world characteristics, the model may learn artefacts and still fail on genuine rare cases

questions.explanation: Synthetic augmentation helps only if it is realistic and diverse; unrealistic samples can teach spurious patterns and give false confidence.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Which check best addresses "data poisoning" risk in a pipeline that ingests user-contributed content?

options.A: Checking the CSS is valid
options.B: Validating, filtering, and anomaly-scanning incoming data, plus tracking data provenance, before it enters the training set

questions.explanation: Poisoning is the deliberate insertion of malicious training data. Provenance tracking, validation, and outlier detection reduce the chance it corrupts the model.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: A tester finds duplicate records that appear in both training and test sets. The immediate quality impact is:

options.A: None
options.B: The test metric is optimistically biased because the model has effectively seen part of the test set

questions.explanation: Cross-set duplicates are a form of leakage: measured test performance overstates true generalisation.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: Which is the most appropriate first response when input data testing reveals that a key feature is missing for 30% of records?

options.A: Silently drop all rows with the missing feature and proceed
options.B: Analyse whether the missingness is random or systematic, quantify its impact, and choose an imputation or handling strategy with stakeholders
options.C: Fill the gaps with zeros without analysis
options.D: Ignore it; models handle missing data automatically

questions.explanation: Systematic missingness can bias the model. The pattern and impact must be understood before deciding to impute, model the missingness, or exclude the feature.

questions.domain: Input Data Testing for ML Systems
questions.question: For an image dataset, which is a valid representativeness check?

options.A: Confirm the images are PNG format
options.B: Compare the distribution of relevant conditions (lighting, angle, device, demographics) in the dataset against expected production conditions
options.C: Confirm each image is exactly 1 MB

questions.explanation: Representativeness means the dataset's coverage of real-world variation matches what the model will encounter live.

questions.question: A monitoring dashboard shows model accuracy has fallen from 0.90 to 0.78 over three months while input distributions look stable. This most likely indicates:

options.A: Data drift
options.B: Concept drift (the input-output relationship has changed)

questions.explanation: Stable inputs but falling accuracy point to concept drift: the true mapping from features to label has shifted, so the model needs retraining on recent data.

questions.question: Which is a correct use of back-to-back testing when migrating a model from framework A to framework B?

options.A: Deploy B and hope for the best
options.B: Run the same input set through both models and investigate any predictions that differ beyond a defined tolerance
options.C: Compare only the model file sizes

questions.explanation: Back-to-back testing across the two implementations should yield near-identical outputs; systematic differences signal a porting defect.

questions.question: A tester wants to detect overfitting during model testing without access to production data. Which approach is valid?

options.A: Compare performance on training data versus a held-out test set and look for a large gap; also use cross-validation stability
options.B: Only look at training accuracy
options.C: Increase the model size until training accuracy is 100%

questions.explanation: A large train-vs-test performance gap, and high variance across cross-validation folds, are the standard indicators of overfitting.

questions.question: Which metamorphic relation is appropriate for testing a sentiment-analysis model?

options.A: Adding a strongly negative sentence to a positive review should not increase the predicted positivity
options.B: Reversing the word order should always keep the same sentiment
options.C: Translating to another language should give the exact same confidence score

questions.explanation: A directional metamorphic relation: making the text more negative should not make the model more positive. A violation reveals an inconsistency defect.

questions.question: During adversarial testing of a text classifier, replacing words with synonyms flips the label. The best classification of this result is:

options.A: Expected behaviour
options.B: A robustness defect: the model relies on brittle surface features rather than meaning

questions.explanation: Synonym substitution preserves meaning; a label flip shows the model is over-sensitive to lexical form, a robustness weakness.

questions.question: Which is the most complete definition of an A/B test's success criterion for a new model?

options.A: The new model has higher offline accuracy
options.B: The new model produces a statistically significant improvement in the pre-defined primary business/quality metric with no unacceptable regression in guardrail metrics
options.D: The new model was trained more recently

questions.explanation: A sound A/B decision requires statistical significance on the primary metric and monitoring of guardrail metrics (latency, complaints, fairness) for regressions.

questions.question: A model performs well overall but poorly on inputs from one hospital in a multi-site deployment. Which model-testing technique surfaces this?

options.A: Aggregate accuracy only
options.B: Slice-based / subgroup evaluation across sites, devices, and demographics

questions.explanation: Evaluating metrics per meaningful slice exposes localised failures that a single aggregate number hides.

questions.question: Which statement about testing model calibration is correct?

options.A: Calibration means the model's file is compressed
options.B: A well-calibrated model's predicted probabilities match observed frequencies (of items predicted at 0.8 confidence, about 80% are correct)
options.C: Calibration is only relevant for regression
options.D: Calibration is the same as accuracy

questions.explanation: Calibration testing (for example reliability diagrams, expected calibration error) checks whether confidence scores can be trusted as probabilities, important when downstream decisions use thresholds.

questions.question: A drift monitor should ideally alert on:

options.A: Only a drop in model accuracy
options.B: Both input feature drift and, where ground truth is available, output/performance drift, with thresholds tuned to avoid alert fatigue

questions.explanation: Effective drift monitoring watches input distributions (available immediately) and delayed performance metrics (once labels arrive), with sensible alert thresholds.

questions.question: Which is a valid reason to reject a model that meets its accuracy target?

options.A: It was trained on a Tuesday
options.B: It fails fairness tolerances, is poorly calibrated, or collapses under mild input perturbation
options.C: It uses more than three features
options.D: It was built by a contractor

questions.explanation: Accuracy is necessary but not sufficient. Fairness, calibration, and robustness failures are legitimate grounds to block release.

questions.question: For a generative model, "exposure bias" during evaluation refers to:

options.A: Too much sunlight on the training images
options.B: A mismatch between training (conditioned on ground-truth tokens) and inference (conditioned on its own previous outputs), which testing on realistic free-running generation helps reveal

questions.explanation: Teacher forcing during training differs from autoregressive inference. Free-running generation tests expose error accumulation that token-level training metrics miss.

questions.question: A team reports "the model passed all its tests" but only ran the same 20 curated examples used during development. The main testing weakness is:

options.A: Too many test cases
options.B: The evaluation set is small, non-representative, and possibly overfit to during development, so results do not predict production behaviour

questions.explanation: Repeatedly tuning against a tiny fixed set overfits the process to it. A larger, representative, and ideally fresh evaluation set is needed.

questions.question: Which is the best description of "regression" in the context of model testing (not the ML task)?

options.A: The model predicting continuous values
options.B: A previously working behaviour or metric degrading after a change to data, features, model, or prompts

questions.explanation: Here "regression" means a quality regression: a change causes formerly acceptable behaviour or scores to worsen, which regression testing is designed to catch.

questions.question: A confusion matrix on the test set shows many false positives for one class. Which follow-up analysis is most useful?

options.A: Delete that class
options.B: Examine the misclassified examples for common patterns (similar features, label noise, under-represented sub-cases) to target a fix
options.D: Retrain with a different random seed only

questions.explanation: Error analysis on the actual misclassified items usually reveals a concrete cause, ambiguous cases, mislabels, or a data gap, that can be addressed.

questions.question: Which is an appropriate guardrail metric to monitor when A/B testing a new ranking model optimised for engagement?

options.A: Only click-through rate
options.B: User complaint rate, content-diversity, and exposure fairness, to catch harmful optimisation of the primary metric

questions.explanation: Optimising engagement can degrade other qualities. Guardrail metrics detect unacceptable side effects even when the primary metric improves.

questions.question: A model shows high variance: retraining with a different random seed changes test accuracy by plus or minus 3%. The correct testing response is:

options.A: Report a single run and ignore the variation
options.B: Report performance as a mean with spread over multiple seeds/runs, and consider it when comparing models against thresholds

questions.explanation: Training stochasticity means a single number is unreliable. Averaging over seeds, and reporting variance, gives a trustworthy comparison.

questions.question: During ML development testing, which risk does verifying the reproducibility of the training pipeline mitigate?

options.A: The website being slow
options.B: Being unable to recreate a released model for debugging, audit, or incident response because data, code, or environment were not versioned
options.C: The model file being too small

questions.explanation: Reproducibility requires versioned data, code, config, and environment. Without it, a production model cannot be rebuilt or investigated reliably.

questions.question: A canary release of a new model routes 5% of traffic to it. Which monitoring result should trigger automatic rollback?

options.A: The canary uses slightly less memory
options.B: A statistically clear degradation in a key metric (errors, latency, complaint rate) on the canary versus control
options.C: The canary was deployed in the afternoon
options.D: The canary model has a newer version number

questions.explanation: Canary analysis compares the small canary slice against the control; a significant adverse difference in guardrail metrics should halt or reverse the rollout.

questions.question: Which is the best example of a CI check for an ML project?

options.A: Only linting the README
options.B: On each change, run data-validation, unit tests for feature transforms, a fast model-quality gate on a fixed evaluation set, and fail the build if metrics drop below a threshold
options.C: Deploy straight to production without tests
options.D: Manually email the results once a month

questions.explanation: An ML CI pipeline automates data checks, transform tests, and a metrics gate so regressions are caught before merge or deploy.

questions.question: Shadow deployment is chosen for a new fraud model. Which limitation must the tester note?

options.A: It cannot generate any logs
options.B: The shadow model's outputs are not acted upon, so effects that depend on taking action (for example blocked transactions changing user behaviour) are not observed
options.C: It always doubles infrastructure cost permanently

questions.explanation: Shadow testing safely compares predictions on live traffic but cannot measure downstream consequences of acting on those predictions.

questions.question: Which practice most reduces the risk of "training/serving skew"?

options.A: Writing the preprocessing twice, once for training and once for serving
options.B: Sharing a single, tested transformation component (or feature store) between training and serving
options.C: Using different libraries in each environment

questions.explanation: A shared, version-controlled transformation path (or feature store) ensures identical feature computation in both training and inference.
